data_analysis.notes: Umbrella-like process concept: the library skills live in lib_pandas; these two problem-based topics teach the workflow and sanity checks. Text analysis (Boot.dev BookBot) is covered by B07 dictionaries.counting_pattern and B10 cli_applications; py4e's spider/visualise pipelines by B16/B17. Portfolio projects (Days 99-100) are multistep material built from these topics.

lib_numpy.notes: Five topics (Day 77): arrays, vectorised ops, indexing, boolean masks, axes/broadcasting/@. Installing numpy (pip/%pip) is third_party_packages.find_and_install and is not a prerequisite: the browser platform is assumed to ship numpy, pandas, matplotlib, seaborn, plotly, scipy and scikit-learn. Images as 3D arrays (Day 77 image manipulation, Day 92 colour palette) are left to B19 image_processing, which can depend on lib_numpy.index_and_slice. np.random.default_rng is used once (statistics_hypothesis_testing.distributions_and_spread) as a recipe line. Snippets were run with NumPy 2.0.2.

lib_pandas.notes: Ten topics (100 Days Days 25-26, 31-32, 72-76). Entry depends on lib_numpy.vectorised_arithmetic so vectorisation and masks are taught once, in NumPy; 100 Days teaches pandas first, so a reviewer may prefer to cut that link. Examples print .tolist() and scalars rather than whole tables, because NumPy 2 scalar reprs (np.int64(12)) and table layout vary by version. pandas was not installed: these snippets were not run; outputs were checked by hand and by recomputing with NumPy. Reading a table from SQL (pd.read_sql) belongs to B17 databases_sql; pd.read_html scraping to B16 web_scraping; Tkinter flash cards (Day 31) use to_python_and_files and belong to B19.

data_visualization.notes: Library-independent chart choice and honesty; the drawing calls are owned by lib_matplotlib, lib_seaborn and lib_plotly. tool_d3js (py4e) is not in this batch's concept list and was not given a topic. Plot topics are graded by matching calls to chart sketches, predicting heights/counts, and fix-the-bug on arguments, since rendered images cannot be compared.

lib_matplotlib.notes: Entry topic needs only lists (MIT L25 plots lists), so it can be taught before pandas. Locators/date formatters (Day 75) were folded into plot_pandas_data practice rather than given a KP. Snippets were not run (matplotlib not installed); the quoted ValueError and TypeError texts are matplotlib's standard messages.

lib_seaborn.notes: Not run (seaborn not installed). regplot leads into linear_regression, but linear_regression does not depend on seaborn: numpy polyfit + matplotlib scatter carry the same idea.

lib_plotly.notes: plotly.express only (Days 76, 79); graph_objects was left out. Not run (plotly not installed).

lib_scipy.notes: One topic on calling scipy.stats; the meaning of tests is owned by statistics_hypothesis_testing. Not run (scipy not installed): the t statistic, p-values and r were recomputed independently with NumPy and numerical integration of the t distribution.

lib_scikit_learn.notes: One topic on the estimator API (fit/predict, 2D X, trailing-underscore attributes, train_test_split). Regression meaning is linear_regression. Not run (scikit-learn not installed); coefficients and R-squared were recomputed with numpy.polyfit/lstsq.

linear_regression.notes: Days 78 and 81. Feature scaling, regularisation and multicollinearity were left out (not taught by any course).

statistics_hypothesis_testing.notes: Day 80 (Semmelweis). p-values are introduced by a shuffling simulation in plain Python (run with 3.13) before scipy, building on B14 simulation_monte_carlo, so the t-test is not a black box. Confidence intervals, chi-squared and one-sided tests were left out.

topics.title: NumPy arrays: making them and reading their shape
topics.summary: Create 1D and 2D NumPy arrays from lists and with arange/zeros/linspace, and read shape, ndim and dtype.

knowledge_points.title: import numpy as np and make an array from a list
knowledge_points.worked_example:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([2, 4, 6])
print(a)          # [2 4 6]
print(len(a), a[0])  # 3 2
np is the standard alias; an array prints without commas.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict what printing an array shows; write the import line and the array for a given list.

knowledge_points.title: 2D arrays: shape, ndim and dtype
knowledge_points.worked_example:
grid = np.array([[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]])
print(grid.shape)  # (2, 3)
print(grid.ndim)   # 2
print(grid.dtype)  # int64
shape is (rows, columns). Rows must be the same length: np.array([[1, 2], [3]])
# ValueError: setting an array element with a sequence. The requested array has an inhomogeneous shape ...
knowledge_points.practice: Predict shape and ndim of nested lists turned into arrays; spot the list that cannot become an array.

knowledge_points.title: Every element has one type
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print(np.array([1, 2.5, 3]))   # [1.  2.5 3. ]
print(np.array([1, 'a']))      # ['1' 'a']
One float turns every element into a float; one string turns them all into strings.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the dtype (int, float or text) of arrays built from mixed lists.

knowledge_points.title: Ready-made arrays: arange, zeros and linspace
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print(np.arange(0, 10, 3))   # [0 3 6 9]
print(np.zeros(3))           # [0. 0. 0.]
print(np.linspace(0, 1, 5))  # [0.   0.25 0.5  0.75 1.  ]
arange is like range (stop excluded); linspace takes a count and includes the stop.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the arrays these calls make; choose arange or linspace for described sequences.

topics.title: Vectorised arithmetic: maths on whole arrays
topics.summary: Apply arithmetic and functions to every element at once, combine equal-length arrays, and summarise with sum/mean/max/argmax.

knowledge_points.title: An operator applies to every element
knowledge_points.worked_example:
prices = np.array([10, 20, 30])
print(prices * 2)        # [20 40 60]
print([10, 20, 30] * 2)  # [10, 20, 30, 10, 20, 30]
The same * repeats a list but doubles each element of an array: no loop needed.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict results of +, *, ** on arrays and the same operator on lists.

knowledge_points.title: Two arrays combine element by element
knowledge_points.worked_example:
a = np.array([1, 2, 3])
b = np.array([10, 20, 30])
print(a + b)  # [11 22 33]
print(b / a)  # [10. 10. 10.]
np.array([1, 2]) + np.array([1, 2, 3])
# ValueError: operands could not be broadcast together with shapes (2,) (3,)
knowledge_points.practice: Predict element-wise results; fix code that combines arrays of different lengths.

knowledge_points.title: Summaries: sum, mean, max and argmax
knowledge_points.worked_example:
temps = np.array([12, 18, 15, 21])
print(temps.sum(), temps.mean(), temps.max())  # 66 16.5 21
print(temps.argmax())  # 3
argmax gives the position of the largest value, not the value.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict summary values; use argmax to find which day was hottest from a parallel list of names.

knowledge_points.title: NumPy functions work on whole arrays; math functions do not
knowledge_points.worked_example:
x = np.array([1, 4, 9])
print(np.sqrt(x))   # [1. 2. 3.]
import math
math.sqrt(x)
# TypeError: only length-1 arrays can be converted to Python scalars
knowledge_points.practice: Replace a loop that rounds or square-roots each item with one NumPy call; fix code that calls math on an array.

topics.title: Indexing and slicing arrays, rows and columns
topics.summary: Index and slice 1D and 2D arrays with [row, col], take whole rows and columns, and know that slices are views of the original.

knowledge_points.title: 1D indexing and slicing work like lists
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the result of indexes and slices with negative positions and steps.

knowledge_points.title: 2D: one bracket, row then column
knowledge_points.worked_example:
grid = np.array([[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]])
print(grid[1, 2])  # 6
print(grid[1][2])  # 6
Both work; grid[r, c] is the NumPy way (grid[r][c] makes a row first).
knowledge_points.practice: Predict single elements of a 2D array; write the index for a described cell.

knowledge_points.title: Whole rows and columns with :
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print(grid[0])      # [1 2 3]
print(grid[:, 1])   # [2 5]
print(grid[:, 1:])  # [[2 3]
                    #  [5 6]]
: means every row (or column). A column needs no loop, unlike a list of lists.
knowledge_points.practice: Write the expression for a given row, column or block; predict sums of a column.

knowledge_points.title: Slices are views: changing one changes the original
knowledge_points.worked_example:
a = np.array([1, 2, 3, 4])
part = a[:2]
part[0] = 99
print(a)   # [99  2  3  4]
A list slice is a copy; an array slice is not. Use a[:2].copy() to get an independent array.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the original array after changing a slice; fix code that must not change its input.

topics.title: Selecting with boolean masks
topics.summary: Compare an array to get a True/False mask, select and count matching elements, combine conditions with & | ~, and use np.where.

knowledge_points.title: A comparison gives an array of booleans
knowledge_points.worked_example:
scores = np.array([55, 72, 90, 40])
print(scores > 60)   # [False  True  True False]
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the mask for comparisons with <, >=, ==.

knowledge_points.title: Use a mask to select and to count
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print(scores[scores > 60])      # [72 90]
print((scores > 60).sum())      # 2
Inside [] a mask keeps the True positions; summing counts the Trues.
knowledge_points.practice: Write the expression that selects or counts the elements meeting a condition.

knowledge_points.title: Combine conditions with & and |, in parentheses
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print(scores[(scores > 50) & (scores < 80)])  # [55 72]
scores[scores > 50 and scores < 80]
# ValueError: The truth value of an array with more than one element is ambiguous. Use a.any() or a.all()
and/or work on single True/False values; & | ~ work element by element. Without parentheses & binds first and gives the same error.
knowledge_points.practice: Fix masks written with and/or or missing parentheses; write a mask for a range or an either-or condition.

knowledge_points.title: np.where and assigning through a mask
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print(np.where(scores >= 60, 'pass', 'fail'))  # ['fail' 'pass' 'pass' 'fail']
scores[scores < 50] = 50
print(scores)   # [55 72 90 50]
knowledge_points.practice: Predict np.where labels; write one line that caps or floors values.

topics.title: Axes, reshaping, broadcasting and matrix multiplication
topics.summary: Summarise a 2D array along axis 0 or 1, reshape arrays, predict broadcasting of a row across rows, and tell element-wise * from matrix @.

knowledge_points.title: Summaries along an axis
knowledge_points.worked_example:
sales = np.array([[3, 5], [4, 1], [2, 2]])   # 3 days x 2 shops
print(sales.sum(axis=0))  # [9 8]    one total per column
print(sales.sum(axis=1))  # [8 5 4]  one total per row
axis=0 collapses the rows; axis=1 collapses the columns.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict per-row and per-column sums, means and maxima; choose the axis for a described total.

knowledge_points.title: Reshaping keeps the elements, changes the shape
knowledge_points.worked_example:
a = np.arange(6)
print(a.reshape(2, 3))  # [[0 1 2]
                        #  [3 4 5]]
a.reshape(4, 2)
# ValueError: cannot reshape array of size 6 into shape (4,2)
knowledge_points.practice: Predict reshaped arrays; pick the shapes a 12-element array can take.

knowledge_points.title: Broadcasting: a row is applied to every row
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print(sales * np.array([2, 10]))  # [[ 6 50]
                                  #  [ 8 10]
                                  #  [ 4 20]]
Shapes (3, 2) and (2,) line up from the right, so the price row is reused for each day.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict broadcast results; decide whether two shapes are compatible.

knowledge_points.title: Matrix multiplication with @ is not *
knowledge_points.practice: Compute small @ products by hand; choose * or @ for a described calculation.

topics.title: pandas Series: labelled columns of data
topics.summary: Create a Series from a list or dict, look values up by label, and use vectorised maths and summaries, including label alignment that produces NaN.

knowledge_points.title: A Series is values plus an index
knowledge_points.worked_example:
import pandas as pd
temps = pd.Series([12, 18, 15])
print(temps)
# 0    12
# 1    18
# 2    15
# dtype: int64
The left column is the index (row labels), not data.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the index and values of a printed Series; write the import line.

knowledge_points.title: Labels from a dict, lookup by label
knowledge_points.worked_example:
temps = pd.Series({'Mon': 12, 'Tue': 18, 'Wed': 15})
print(temps['Tue'])       # 18
print(list(temps.index))  # ['Mon', 'Tue', 'Wed']
temps['Fri']
# KeyError: 'Fri'
knowledge_points.practice: Predict lookups, including a missing label; build a Series from a dict.

knowledge_points.title: Maths and summaries work like NumPy
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print(temps.mean())                  # 15.0
print((temps * 2)['Wed'])            # 30
print(temps.max(), temps.idxmax())   # 18 Tue
idxmax returns the label of the largest value.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict results of arithmetic and summaries; find the label of the minimum.

knowledge_points.title: Two Series line up by label; gaps become NaN
knowledge_points.worked_example:
a = pd.Series({'x': 1, 'y': 2})
b = pd.Series({'y': 10, 'z': 20})
print((a + b).tolist())  # [nan, 12.0, nan]
Only 'y' is in both; NaN (not a number) marks the missing results.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the result of adding Series with partly different labels.

topics.title: DataFrames: building, loading and inspecting tables
topics.summary: Build a DataFrame from a dict of lists or read_csv, and inspect it with shape, columns, head, dtypes and describe.

knowledge_points.title: A DataFrame from a dict of lists
knowledge_points.worked_example:
df = pd.DataFrame({'name': ['Ana', 'Bo', 'Cy'], 'age': [31, 27, 45]})
print(df.shape)          # (3, 2)
print(list(df.columns))  # ['name', 'age']
Each key becomes a column; every list must have the same length.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict shape and columns; write the dict that builds a described table.

knowledge_points.title: Load a CSV file with read_csv
knowledge_points.worked_example:
# weather.csv
# day,temp,rain
# Mon,12,0.0
# Tue,18,2.5
# Wed,15,0.0
df = pd.read_csv('weather.csv')
print(df.shape)          # (3, 3)
print(list(df.columns))  # ['day', 'temp', 'rain']
The header row becomes column names and numbers are converted for you, unlike csv.reader.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the shape and columns read from a short CSV; compare with the csv.reader version.

knowledge_points.title: Look before you analyse: head, dtypes, describe
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print(df.head(2))              # first 2 rows
print(df['temp'].dtype)        # int64
print(df['rain'].dtype)        # float64
print(df['temp'].describe()['mean'])  # 15.0
In Jupyter, a cell ending in df.head() shows a formatted table; describe() gives count, mean, std, min, quartiles, max.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict dtypes of columns from CSV text; read values off a describe() table.

knowledge_points.title: Column names must match exactly
knowledge_points.worked_example:
df['Temp']
# KeyError: 'Temp'
print(list(df.columns))   # check the real names first
Case and spaces count: ' temp' is not 'temp'.
knowledge_points.practice: Fix KeyErrors caused by case, spaces or typos in column names.

topics.title: Selecting columns and rows: [], loc and iloc
topics.summary: Select one or several columns, rows by position with iloc and by label with loc, and know that loc slices include the end.

knowledge_points.title: One column is a Series; a list of columns is a DataFrame
knowledge_points.worked_example:
# weather.csv
# day,temp,rain
# Mon,12,0.0
# Tue,18,2.5
# Wed,15,0.0
temps = df['temp']
print(temps.max())            # 18
sub = df[['day', 'temp']]
print(sub.shape)              # (3, 2)
df['day', 'temp']
# KeyError: ('day', 'temp')
knowledge_points.practice: Predict whether a selection gives a Series or DataFrame; fix the missing inner brackets.

knowledge_points.title: Rows by position with iloc
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print(df.iloc[0]['day'])     # Mon
print(df.iloc[-1]['temp'])   # 15
print(df.iloc[0:2].shape)    # (2, 3)
iloc uses positions like list indexes; the end of a slice is excluded.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict iloc lookups and slice sizes.

knowledge_points.title: Rows and columns by label with loc
knowledge_points.worked_example:
byday = df.set_index('day')
print(byday.loc['Tue', 'temp'])               # 18
print(byday.loc['Mon':'Tue', 'rain'].sum())   # 2.5
loc[row label, column name]; a label slice includes its end.
knowledge_points.practice: Write loc expressions for described cells and ranges; predict sums over label slices.

knowledge_points.title: loc vs iloc on a numbered index
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print(len(df.loc[0:1]), len(df.iloc[0:1]))   # 2 1
With the default 0, 1, 2 index both look alike, but loc includes the end label and iloc excludes the end position.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict row counts of loc/iloc slices; choose loc or iloc for a described selection.

topics.title: Filtering rows with conditions
topics.summary: Keep rows matching a condition, combine conditions with & | ~, use isin and str.contains, and select or change matching rows with .loc[mask, col].

knowledge_points.title: A boolean mask keeps matching rows
knowledge_points.worked_example:
# weather.csv
# day,temp,rain
# Mon,12,0.0
# Tue,18,2.5
# Wed,15,0.0
warm = df[df['temp'] > 14]
print(warm['day'].tolist())   # ['Tue', 'Wed']
df['temp'] > 14 is a Series of True/False, one per row.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict which rows a mask keeps; write the filter for a described condition.

knowledge_points.title: Combine conditions with &, | and ~
knowledge_points.worked_example:
dry_warm = df[(df['temp'] > 14) & (df['rain'] == 0)]
print(dry_warm['day'].tolist())   # ['Wed']
df[df['temp'] > 14 and df['rain'] == 0]
# ValueError: The truth value of a Series is ambiguous. ...
knowledge_points.practice: Fix filters that use and/or or lack parentheses; write a filter with ~ (not).

knowledge_points.title: isin and text conditions with .str
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print(df[df['day'].isin(['Mon', 'Wed'])]['temp'].tolist())   # [12, 15]
print(len(df[df['day'].str.contains('e')]))                   # 2
isin replaces a chain of == ... |; .str applies string methods to every row.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict row counts for isin and str.contains filters; rewrite an | chain with isin.

knowledge_points.title: Select or change only matching rows with .loc[mask, column]
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print(df.loc[df['rain'] > 0, 'day'].tolist())   # ['Tue']
df.loc[df['temp'] < 13, 'temp'] = 13
print(df['temp'].tolist())                       # [13, 18, 15]
knowledge_points.practice: Write .loc lines that read or overwrite a column for matching rows; predict the column afterwards.

topics.title: Sorting rows and adding new columns
topics.summary: Sort by a column, find top rows and the row of a maximum, add a column computed from others, and remember that most methods return a new table.

knowledge_points.title: sort_values, ascending or descending
knowledge_points.worked_example:
# weather.csv
# day,temp,rain
# Mon,12,0.0
# Tue,18,2.5
# Wed,15,0.0
print(df.sort_values('temp')['day'].tolist())                   # ['Mon', 'Wed', 'Tue']
print(df.sort_values('temp', ascending=False)['day'].tolist())  # ['Tue', 'Wed', 'Mon']
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the order after sorting by a column, ascending and descending.

knowledge_points.title: The top rows and the row of the maximum
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print(df.loc[df['temp'].idxmax(), 'day'])       # Tue
print(df.nlargest(2, 'temp')['day'].tolist())   # ['Tue', 'Wed']
idxmax gives the row label; loc then reads another column of that row.
knowledge_points.practice: Write the expression for 'which X has the highest Y'; predict nlargest/nsmallest results.

knowledge_points.title: A new column computed from others
knowledge_points.worked_example:
df['feels'] = df['temp'] - df['rain'] * 2
print(df['feels'].tolist())   # [12.0, 13.0, 15.0]
Assigning to a new column name adds it; the maths runs row by row without a loop.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict a derived column; write the line that adds a ratio or difference column.

knowledge_points.title: Methods return a new table: assign the result
knowledge_points.worked_example:
df.sort_values('temp')
df.drop(columns=['rain'])
print('rain' in df.columns)   # True: nothing changed
df = df.drop(columns=['rain'])   # keep the result
Like sorted(), these return a new DataFrame; rename(columns={'temp': 'temp_c'}) works the same way.
knowledge_points.practice: Fix code whose sort, drop or rename has no effect; predict shapes after a sequence of calls.

topics.title: Cleaning data: missing values, duplicates and text numbers
topics.summary: Count and handle missing values with isna/dropna/fillna, remove duplicate rows, and turn text like '1,000+' into numbers.

knowledge_points.title: Find missing values
knowledge_points.worked_example:
df = pd.DataFrame({'city': ['Oslo', 'Rome', None], 'pop': [1.5, None, 2.5]})
print(df.isna().sum().tolist())   # [1, 1]
print(df['pop'].mean())             # 2.0
Missing values show as NaN (or None); summaries skip them.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict missing-value counts per column and summaries that skip NaN.

knowledge_points.title: Drop or fill missing values
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print(len(df.dropna()))                # 1
print(df['pop'].fillna(0).tolist())   # [1.5, 0.0, 2.5]
dropna removes any row with a NaN in any column; fillna replaces NaN with a value.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict row counts after dropna; choose dropna or fillna for a described situation and write it.

knowledge_points.title: Duplicate rows
knowledge_points.worked_example:
df = pd.DataFrame({'name': ['Ana', 'Bo', 'Ana'], 'score': [3, 5, 3]})
print(df.duplicated().tolist())   # [False, False, True]
print(len(df.drop_duplicates()))  # 2
duplicated marks repeats of an earlier row; subset=['name'] compares only that column.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict duplicated() masks with and without subset; write the de-duplication line.

knowledge_points.title: Text that should be numbers
knowledge_points.worked_example:
installs = pd.Series(['1,000+', '50+', '500+'])
clean = installs.str.replace(',', '').str.replace('+', '')
print(pd.to_numeric(clean).sum())   # 1550
Without cleaning, the column holds strings and cannot be summed as numbers. errors='coerce' turns leftovers like 'Free' into NaN.
knowledge_points.practice: Write the chain that strips symbols and converts; fix code that compares or sums a text column.

topics.title: Grouping and aggregating: groupby, value_counts and pivot tables
topics.summary: Split rows into groups and summarise each with groupby, count rows per group, compute several aggregates, and cross-tabulate with pivot_table.

knowledge_points.title: groupby one column, summarise another
knowledge_points.worked_example:
sales = pd.DataFrame({'shop': ['A', 'B', 'A', 'B', 'A'],
                      'item': ['tea', 'tea', 'cake', 'cake', 'tea'],
                      'amount': [3, 5, 4, 1, 2]})
totals = sales.groupby('shop')['amount'].sum()
print(totals['A'], totals['B'])   # 9 6
One line replaces the dict-of-lists grouping loop; the result is a Series indexed by shop.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict per-group sums and means; write the groupby for a described question.

knowledge_points.title: Counting rows per group
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print(sales['shop'].value_counts()['A'])     # 3
print(sales.groupby('item').size()['tea'])   # 3
value_counts counts each value of one column, largest first.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict counts; choose value_counts, size or sum for 'how many' vs 'how much' questions.

knowledge_points.title: Several aggregates at once with agg
knowledge_points.worked_example:
summary = sales.groupby('shop')['amount'].agg(['sum', 'mean', 'count'])
print(summary.loc['A', 'mean'])   # 3.0
The result is a DataFrame: one row per group, one column per aggregate; sort it with sort_values.
knowledge_points.practice: Read values from an agg table; write an agg call and sort the groups by one aggregate.

knowledge_points.title: Two keys: pivot_table
knowledge_points.worked_example:
table = sales.pivot_table(index='shop', columns='item', values='amount', aggfunc='sum')
print(table.loc['A', 'tea'])   # 5
sales.pivot(index='shop', columns='item', values='amount')
# ValueError: Index contains duplicate entries, cannot reshape
pivot only reshapes; pivot_table also aggregates repeats.
knowledge_points.practice: Fill in a pivot table by hand from raw rows; fix a pivot that fails on duplicates.

topics.title: Combining tables with merge
topics.summary: Join two DataFrames on a key column (primary/foreign keys), handle different key names, keep unmatched rows with how='left', and catch rows multiplied by duplicate keys.

knowledge_points.title: merge on a shared key column
knowledge_points.worked_example:
sets = pd.DataFrame({'name': ['Castle', 'Ship', 'Car'], 'theme_id': [1, 2, 9]})
themes = pd.DataFrame({'theme_id': [1, 2, 3], 'theme': ['Medieval', 'Pirates', 'Space']})
m = pd.merge(sets, themes, on='theme_id')
print(m['theme'].tolist())   # ['Medieval', 'Pirates']
The default inner join keeps only keys found in both tables (Car's 9 is dropped).
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the rows of an inner merge; write the merge for two given tables.

knowledge_points.title: Keys with different names: left_on and right_on
knowledge_points.worked_example:
themes = themes.rename(columns={'theme_id': 'id'})
m = pd.merge(sets, themes, left_on='theme_id', right_on='id')
id is the primary key of themes (unique); theme_id in sets is a foreign key pointing at it.
knowledge_points.practice: Identify primary and foreign keys in two tables; fill in left_on/right_on.

knowledge_points.title: how='left' keeps unmatched rows as NaN
knowledge_points.worked_example:
m = pd.merge(sets, themes, left_on='theme_id', right_on='id', how='left')
print(len(m), m['theme'].isna().sum())   # 3 1
knowledge_points.practice: Predict row counts and NaNs for inner vs left merges.

knowledge_points.title: Duplicate keys multiply rows: check the count
knowledge_points.worked_example:
dup = pd.DataFrame({'id': [1, 1], 'theme': ['Medieval', 'Castles']})
m = pd.merge(sets, dup, left_on='theme_id', right_on='id', how='left')
print(len(m))   # 4, from a 3-row table
Compare len() before and after; a lookup table needs unique keys.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict row counts when keys repeat; find the duplicated key that inflated a merged total.

topics.title: Dates and time series in pandas
topics.summary: Convert text to datetimes, extract parts with .dt, total by month with groupby or resample, and smooth with a rolling mean.

knowledge_points.title: pd.to_datetime and the .dt accessor
knowledge_points.worked_example:
df = pd.DataFrame({'date': ['2024-01-15', '2024-02-03', '2024-02-20'], 'posts': [5, 8, 3]})
df['date'] = pd.to_datetime(df['date'])
print(df['date'].dt.month.tolist())   # [1, 2, 2]
As text, '2024-9-1' sorts after '2024-10-1'; as datetimes they compare correctly.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict .dt.year/.dt.month values; fix sorting or filtering that treats dates as text.

knowledge_points.title: Totals per month with groupby
knowledge_points.worked_example:
monthly = df.groupby(df['date'].dt.month)['posts'].sum()
print(monthly[2])   # 11
knowledge_points.practice: Write the groupby for per-year or per-month totals; predict the totals.

knowledge_points.title: resample on a date index
knowledge_points.worked_example:
s = df.set_index('date')['posts']
print(s.resample('MS').sum().tolist())   # [5, 11]
resample groups by calendar period ('MS' month start, 'YS' year start) and includes empty periods; it needs dates in the index.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict resampled totals, including an empty month; fix resample called on a non-date index.

knowledge_points.title: Smoothing with a rolling mean
knowledge_points.worked_example:
s = pd.Series([2, 4, 6, 8])
print(s.rolling(window=2).mean().tolist())   # [nan, 3.0, 5.0, 7.0]
Each value averages the last 2; the first window - 1 values are NaN.
knowledge_points.practice: Compute rolling means by hand; predict how many NaNs a window size leaves.

topics.title: Between pandas, plain Python and files
topics.summary: Turn columns and rows into lists and dicts (tolist, to_dict, iterrows) for ordinary Python code, and save a DataFrame with to_csv without an extra index column.

knowledge_points.title: Columns to lists and lookup dicts
knowledge_points.worked_example:
# weather.csv
# day,temp,rain
# Mon,12,0.0
# Tue,18,2.5
# Wed,15,0.0
days = df['day'].tolist()            # ['Mon', 'Tue', 'Wed']
lookup = dict(zip(df['day'], df['temp']))
print(lookup['Tue'])                 # 18
knowledge_points.practice: Write the line that turns two columns into a lookup dict; predict lookups.

knowledge_points.title: Rows as a list of dicts
knowledge_points.practice: Predict an element of to_dict(orient='records'); loop over the records to print a report.

knowledge_points.title: Looping over rows with iterrows
knowledge_points.worked_example:
for index, row in df.iterrows():
    print(row['day'], row['temp'])
# Mon 12
# Tue 18
# Wed 15
code = {row['day']: row['temp'] for (index, row) in df.iterrows()}
Prefer vectorised column maths; loop only when each row needs ordinary Python.
knowledge_points.practice: Write a dict comprehension over iterrows; rewrite a row loop as one column expression.

knowledge_points.title: Saving with to_csv(index=False)
knowledge_points.worked_example:
df.to_csv('out.csv')
print(list(pd.read_csv('out.csv').columns))
# ['Unnamed: 0', 'day', 'temp', 'rain']
df.to_csv('out.csv', index=False)   # no extra index column
knowledge_points.practice: Fix a save/load round trip that grows an 'Unnamed: 0' column.

topics.title: From a question to an answer: the analysis workflow
topics.summary: Order the steps of an analysis (load, inspect, clean, transform, answer), translate a question into the pandas operation that answers it, and report shares with the mean of a mask.

knowledge_points.title: Load, inspect, clean, transform, answer
knowledge_points.worked_example:
df = pd.read_csv('majors.csv')            # load
print(df.shape)                           # inspect
df = df.dropna()                          # clean
df['spread'] = df['p90'] - df['p10']      # transform
print(df.nsmallest(3, 'spread')['major'].tolist())   # answer
In a notebook, each step is its own cell so you can look at the result.
knowledge_points.practice: Put the cells of a short analysis in order; find the step that was skipped when a result is wrong.

knowledge_points.title: Match the question to the operation
knowledge_points.worked_example:
df = pd.DataFrame({'group': ['STEM', 'Arts', 'STEM', 'Arts'], 'salary': [60, 40, 70, 42]})
# Which group earns most on average?
print(df.groupby('group')['salary'].mean().idxmax())   # STEM
'Which most' -> idxmax/nlargest; 'how many per' -> value_counts; 'average per' -> groupby mean.
knowledge_points.practice: For each question, choose and then write the pandas expression that answers it.

knowledge_points.title: Shares and percentages from a mask
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print((df['salary'] > 50).mean())   # 0.5
True counts as 1, so the mean of a mask is the share of rows that match; * 100 gives a percentage.
knowledge_points.practice: Write expressions for 'what fraction of rows...'; predict shares for small tables.

topics.title: Checking an analysis: counts, outliers and correlation
topics.summary: Check row counts through each step, notice tiny groups and outliers (mean vs median), and measure a relationship with corr without claiming causation.

knowledge_points.title: Count rows after every step
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print(len(df))
df = df.dropna()
print(len(df))
summary = df.groupby('group')['salary'].agg(['mean', 'count'])
A filter, dropna or merge that silently changes the row count changes every answer; a mean of 2 rows says little.
knowledge_points.practice: Given row counts at each step, find the step that lost or duplicated rows; decide which group means to trust.

knowledge_points.title: An outlier pulls the mean, not the median
knowledge_points.worked_example:
pay = pd.Series([30, 32, 35, 31, 400])
print(pay.mean(), pay.median())   # 105.6 32.0
Check max() and describe(); report the median for skewed data such as salaries or prices.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict mean and median with and without an outlier; choose which to report.

knowledge_points.title: Correlation: how strongly two columns move together
knowledge_points.worked_example:
x = pd.Series([1, 2, 3, 4])
print(round(x.corr(pd.Series([2, 4, 6, 8])), 2))   # 1.0
print(round(x.corr(pd.Series([8, 6, 4, 2])), 2))   # -1.0
corr runs from -1 to 1. Ice-cream sales correlate with sunburn, but neither causes the other: hot weather drives both.
knowledge_points.practice: Match scatter descriptions to correlation values; judge whether a claimed cause follows from a correlation.

topics.title: Line charts with matplotlib
topics.summary: Draw a line chart from two lists, label it, plot several lines with a legend, and fix the length-mismatch error.

knowledge_points.title: plot(x, y) then show()
knowledge_points.worked_example:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
years = [2020, 2021, 2022]
users = [5, 9, 14]
plt.plot(years, users)
plt.show()
x values first, y values second; each (x, y) pair is a point and the points are joined by lines.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the coordinates of the plotted points; write the plot call for two given lists.

knowledge_points.title: Title and axis labels
knowledge_points.worked_example:
plt.plot(years, users)
plt.title('Users per year')
plt.xlabel('Year')
plt.ylabel('Users (thousands)')
plt.show()
knowledge_points.practice: Fill in the missing label calls to match a described chart; spot the label put on the wrong axis.

knowledge_points.title: Several lines with label= and legend()
knowledge_points.worked_example:
plt.plot(years, users, label='App')
plt.plot(years, [3, 4, 4], label='Web')
plt.legend()
plt.show()
Each plot call adds a line; without label= the legend has nothing to show.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict how many lines and legend entries a script draws; fix a legend that comes out empty.

knowledge_points.title: plot(y) alone, and the length-mismatch error
knowledge_points.worked_example:
plt.plot(users)          # x is 0, 1, 2
plt.plot([1, 2, 3], [4, 5])
# ValueError: x and y must have same first dimension, but have shapes (3,) and (2,)
A format string styles the line: plt.plot(years, users, 'o--') draws dots joined by dashes.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the x positions when only y is given; fix mismatched lists.

topics.title: Bar charts, scatter plots, histograms and pies
topics.summary: Draw bar, scatter, histogram and pie charts, predict which chart a call draws, and work out histogram bar heights from raw values.

knowledge_points.title: Bar charts compare categories
knowledge_points.worked_example:
plt.bar(['Tea', 'Cake', 'Pie'], [5, 3, 7])
plt.show()
One bar per category; heights are given. plt.barh draws them sideways for long names.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the tallest bar; write the bar call from a dict of counts (keys and values).

knowledge_points.title: Scatter plots show pairs without joining them
knowledge_points.worked_example:
heights = [150, 160, 170, 180]
weights = [50, 58, 66, 80]
plt.scatter(heights, weights)
plt.show()
Use scatter when order means nothing; plot would draw a misleading line through the points.
knowledge_points.practice: Choose plot or scatter for described data; predict where a given point appears.

knowledge_points.title: Histograms count values into bins
knowledge_points.worked_example:
ages = [21, 22, 25, 31, 33, 38, 45]
plt.hist(ages, bins=[20, 30, 40, 50])
plt.show()
# bar heights: 3, 3, 1
hist takes raw values and does the counting; bar takes counts you already have.
knowledge_points.practice: Compute histogram bar heights from raw values and bin edges; fix a bar() call given raw values.

knowledge_points.title: Which call draws which chart?
knowledge_points.worked_example:
plt.pie([3, 1], labels=['Yes', 'No'])   # a circle, 3/4 and 1/4
plt.plot(x, y)     -> line
plt.bar(x, h)      -> bars
plt.scatter(x, y)  -> dots
plt.hist(values)   -> bars of counts
knowledge_points.practice: Match calls to sketches of charts; pick the call that draws a described chart.

topics.title: Figures and axes: subplots, limits and two y-axes
topics.summary: Use fig, ax = plt.subplots() and ax.set_* methods, lay out a grid of charts, add a second y-axis with twinx, set limits and ticks, and save to a file.

knowledge_points.title: fig, ax = plt.subplots() and the ax methods
knowledge_points.worked_example:
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4))
ax.plot(years, users)
ax.set_title('Users')
ax.set_xlabel('Year')
ax.title('Users')
# TypeError: 'Text' object is not callable
plt.title becomes ax.set_title, plt.xlabel becomes ax.set_xlabel.
knowledge_points.practice: Translate plt.* code into ax.* code; fix ax calls missing set_.

knowledge_points.title: A grid of charts
knowledge_points.worked_example:
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2)
axes[0].bar(['a', 'b'], [3, 5])
axes[1].hist(ages)
With plt.subplots(2, 2), pick a chart with axes[row, col].
knowledge_points.practice: Predict which panel each call draws in; write the index of a described panel.

knowledge_points.title: Two y-axes with twinx
knowledge_points.worked_example:
fig, ax1 = plt.subplots()
ax2 = ax1.twinx()
ax1.plot(dates, price, color='red')
ax2.plot(dates, searches, color='blue')
Both lines share the x-axis; each gets its own y scale, so colour each axis label to match its line.
knowledge_points.practice: Choose when two series need two y-axes; fix code that draws both series on ax1.

knowledge_points.title: Limits, ticks and saving
knowledge_points.worked_example:
ax.set_ylim(0, 100)
ax.tick_params(axis='x', rotation=45)
fig.savefig('chart.png', dpi=150)
Save before plt.show(): once the window closes the figure may be empty.
knowledge_points.practice: Fill in limits and rotation for a described chart; order the lines of a save-and-show script.

topics.title: Plotting pandas data with matplotlib
topics.summary: Plot DataFrame columns against dates, draw one line per column of a pivot table, plot rolling means, and use the df.plot shortcut.

knowledge_points.title: Columns as x and y
knowledge_points.worked_example:
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot(df['date'], df['posts'])
ax.set_ylabel('Posts')
Convert dates with pd.to_datetime first, or matplotlib treats them as text labels.
knowledge_points.practice: Write the plot call for two named columns; fix a chart whose dates are plotted as text.

knowledge_points.title: One line per column of a pivoted table
knowledge_points.worked_example:
table = df.pivot_table(index='date', columns='language', values='posts', aggfunc='sum')
for col in table.columns:
    ax.plot(table.index, table[col], label=col)
ax.legend()
knowledge_points.practice: Predict how many lines and legend entries the loop draws; fill in the loop body.

knowledge_points.title: Plotting a Series uses its index as x; smoothing with rolling
knowledge_points.worked_example:
smooth = table['python'].rolling(window=6).mean()
ax.plot(smooth)
The dates in the index become the x values; a 6-period rolling mean hides month-to-month noise.
knowledge_points.practice: Choose a window size for a described smoothing; predict where the smoothed line starts.

knowledge_points.title: The df.plot shortcut
knowledge_points.worked_example:
ax = df.plot(x='date', y='posts', kind='line')
counts.plot(kind='bar')
pandas calls matplotlib for you and returns the ax, so ax.set_title still works.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict which chart a df.plot(kind=...) call draws; rewrite an ax.plot call as df.plot.

topics.title: Choosing the right chart for the question
topics.summary: Pick a line, bar, histogram/box, scatter or pie chart from what the question asks and the shape of the data.

knowledge_points.title: Change over time -> line; compare categories -> bar
knowledge_points.worked_example:
Monthly posts per language    -> plt.plot(months, posts)
Total sales per shop          -> plt.bar(shops, totals)
Sort the bars (sort_values) so the ranking is visible at a glance.
knowledge_points.practice: For described questions, choose line or bar and write the call.

knowledge_points.title: How values are spread -> histogram or box plot
knowledge_points.worked_example:
Distribution of app ratings   -> plt.hist(df['rating'], bins=20)
Ratings for free vs paid apps -> a box plot per group
A bar of the mean hides the spread; a histogram shows it.
knowledge_points.practice: Choose a chart for distribution questions; explain what a mean-only bar chart hides.

knowledge_points.title: Two numbers per row -> scatter; parts of a whole -> pie
knowledge_points.worked_example:
Budget vs revenue per film     -> plt.scatter(df['budget'], df['revenue'])
Share of apps per content rating -> pie or donut, only with a few slices
More than about 5 slices: use a sorted bar chart instead.
knowledge_points.practice: Match questions to chart types across all five kinds; fix a pie chart with too many slices.

topics.title: Making charts honest and readable
topics.summary: Label axes with units, avoid truncated y-axes that exaggerate differences, use a log scale for data spanning orders of magnitude, and reduce clutter.

knowledge_points.title: Every chart needs a title, axis labels and units
knowledge_points.worked_example:
ax.set_title('Revenue by year')
ax.set_xlabel('Year')
ax.set_ylabel('Revenue (USD millions)')
A reader should not have to guess what an axis measures.
knowledge_points.practice: Find what is missing from described charts; fill in the labels.

knowledge_points.title: Bar charts start at zero
knowledge_points.worked_example:
ax.bar(['A', 'B'], [98, 100])
ax.set_ylim(95, 101)   # B looks 3 times taller than A
ax.set_ylim(0, 105)    # the honest view: a 2% difference
knowledge_points.practice: Judge whether an axis range misleads; fix the limits.

knowledge_points.title: Log scale for values spanning orders of magnitude
knowledge_points.worked_example:
ax.scatter(df['installs'], df['rating'])
ax.set_xscale('log')
On a linear axis apps with 1,000 and 100,000 installs are squashed against zero; on a log axis each power of 10 gets equal space.
knowledge_points.practice: Decide when a log axis helps; read values off a log axis.

knowledge_points.title: Reduce clutter: fewer lines, smoothed noise
knowledge_points.worked_example:
top5 = totals.nlargest(5).index
for lang in top5:
    ax.plot(table.index, table[lang].rolling(6).mean(), label=lang)
Twenty overlapping lines are unreadable; keep the top few and smooth the noise.
knowledge_points.practice: Choose how to simplify a cluttered chart; write the line that keeps the top n categories.

topics.title: Seaborn scatter, bubble and regression plots
topics.summary: Draw scatter plots from DataFrame columns with data=, x=, y=, add hue and size to make bubble charts, overlay a regression line with regplot, and style through the returned ax.

knowledge_points.title: scatterplot with data=, x= and y=
knowledge_points.worked_example:
import seaborn as sns
sns.scatterplot(data=df, x='budget', y='revenue')
plt.show()
Columns are named as strings; seaborn looks them up in data.
knowledge_points.practice: Write the seaborn call for two named columns; fix a call whose column name has the wrong case.

knowledge_points.title: hue and size: colour and bubble size from columns
knowledge_points.worked_example:
sns.scatterplot(data=df, x='budget', y='revenue', hue='genre', size='votes')
hue colours each point by a column; size scales it, making a bubble chart.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict what colour and size encode in a described call; fill in hue/size for a target chart.

knowledge_points.title: regplot: scatter plus a best-fit line
knowledge_points.worked_example:
sns.regplot(data=df, x='budget', y='revenue', scatter_kws={'alpha': 0.4}, line_kws={'color': 'red'})
The shaded band around the line shows the uncertainty of the fit.
knowledge_points.practice: Choose scatterplot or regplot for a question; fill in styling keyword dicts.

knowledge_points.title: Seaborn draws on matplotlib axes
knowledge_points.worked_example:
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4))
sns.scatterplot(data=df, x='budget', y='revenue', ax=ax)
ax.set(xlabel='Budget ($)', ylabel='Revenue ($)')
with sns.axes_style('darkgrid'): applies a style to the charts drawn inside the with block.
knowledge_points.practice: Combine seaborn calls with ax methods to match a described chart; order the lines.

topics.title: Seaborn distributions and category plots
topics.summary: Show distributions with histplot/kdeplot, compare groups with hue and box plots, and predict bar heights of barplot (mean) vs countplot (count).

knowledge_points.title: histplot with a KDE curve
knowledge_points.worked_example:
sns.histplot(data=df, x='rating', bins=20, kde=True)
The KDE is a smoothed outline of the histogram: where values are dense, the curve is high.
knowledge_points.practice: Match histograms to KDE curves; pick the column a histplot needs.

knowledge_points.title: Comparing groups with hue
knowledge_points.worked_example:
sns.kdeplot(data=df, x='pct_deaths', hue='washing', fill=True)
One curve per group on the same axes shows whether the distributions shifted.
knowledge_points.practice: Read which group has higher typical values from overlaid curves; fill in hue.

knowledge_points.title: Box plots: median, middle half and outliers
knowledge_points.worked_example:
sns.boxplot(data=df, x='type', y='price')
The line is the median, the box holds the middle 50% of values, dots beyond the whiskers are outliers.
knowledge_points.practice: Read medians and spread from box plots; compute a median to predict the line position.

knowledge_points.title: barplot shows a mean; countplot shows a count
knowledge_points.worked_example:
small = pd.DataFrame({'x': ['a', 'a', 'b'], 'y': [2, 4, 5]})
sns.barplot(data=small, x='x', y='y')   # heights: a 3, b 5
sns.countplot(data=small, x='x')        # heights: a 2, b 1
knowledge_points.practice: Predict bar heights for barplot and countplot on small tables.

topics.title: Interactive charts with plotly.express: bar, pie and donut
topics.summary: Make interactive bar, pie and donut charts with plotly.express from lists or value_counts results, and set titles and labels with update_layout/update_traces.

knowledge_points.title: px.bar and fig.show()
knowledge_points.worked_example:
import plotly.express as px
fig = px.bar(x=['Tea', 'Cake'], y=[5, 3])
fig.show()
The chart is interactive: hover shows values, drag zooms. Every px function returns a fig.
knowledge_points.practice: Translate a plt.bar call into px.bar; predict what hovering over a bar shows.

knowledge_points.title: Charts from value_counts
knowledge_points.worked_example:
counts = df['category'].value_counts()
fig = px.bar(x=counts.index, y=counts.values, color=counts.values)
The index holds the categories and .values the counts; color= shades bars by a number.
knowledge_points.practice: Write the px.bar call for a counts Series; predict the order of the bars.

knowledge_points.title: Pie and donut charts
knowledge_points.worked_example:
fig = px.pie(names=counts.index, values=counts.values, hole=0.6)
names labels the slices, values sizes them; hole turns the pie into a donut.
knowledge_points.practice: Fix a pie with names and values swapped; fill in hole for a donut.

knowledge_points.title: Titles and labels with update_layout and update_traces
knowledge_points.worked_example:
fig.update_layout(title='Apps per category', xaxis_title='Category', yaxis_title='Apps')
fig.update_traces(textposition='outside', textinfo='percent+label')   # for a pie
knowledge_points.practice: Fill in update_layout arguments to match a target chart; choose the update method for a described change.

topics.title: Plotly scatter and box charts: colour, size, hover and log axes
topics.summary: Build plotly scatter and box charts from DataFrame columns with color, size and hover_name, switch an axis to log scale, and group bars by colour.

knowledge_points.title: px.scatter from a DataFrame
knowledge_points.worked_example:
fig = px.scatter(df, x='installs', y='rating', size='reviews', color='category', hover_name='app')
Pass the DataFrame first and name columns; hover_name shows each point's label on hover.
knowledge_points.practice: Fill in the arguments that produce a described bubble chart; predict what the hover box shows.

knowledge_points.title: A log axis
knowledge_points.worked_example:
fig.update_layout(xaxis_type='log')
Installs range from 1 to 1,000,000,000; a log axis spreads them out.
knowledge_points.practice: Choose which axis needs a log scale; write the update_layout line.

knowledge_points.title: Box plots by group
knowledge_points.worked_example:
paid = df[df['type'] == 'Paid']
fig = px.box(df, x='type', y='installs', color='type', points='all', notched=True)
One box per group; points='all' shows every app beside its box.
knowledge_points.practice: Read which group has the higher median; write a filter and box call for a subgroup.

knowledge_points.title: Grouped bars by colour
knowledge_points.worked_example:
fig = px.bar(counts_df, x='genre', y='apps', color='type', barmode='group')
color splits each bar by a column; barmode='group' puts them side by side instead of stacked.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict stacked vs grouped results; fill in color and barmode.

topics.title: Maps and nested charts: choropleth and sunburst
topics.summary: Colour countries on a choropleth map from ISO country codes, prepare per-country counts with groupby, and draw a sunburst whose rings follow a path of columns.

knowledge_points.title: Choropleth maps need ISO codes
knowledge_points.worked_example:
fig = px.choropleth(df, locations='iso_code', color='prizes', hover_name='country', color_continuous_scale='matter')
locations must be 3-letter ISO codes ('USA', 'GBR'); full names like 'United Kingdom' leave countries blank.
knowledge_points.practice: Fix a map that shows no countries; fill in the arguments for a target map.

knowledge_points.title: Prepare counts per country
knowledge_points.worked_example:
per_country = df.groupby(['country', 'iso_code'], as_index=False)['prize'].count()
fig = px.choropleth(per_country, locations='iso_code', color='prize')
The map needs one row per country; merge in codes from a lookup table if they are missing.
knowledge_points.practice: Order the lines that count rows per country and draw the map; choose the groupby keys.

knowledge_points.title: Sunburst: rings follow the path
knowledge_points.worked_example:
fig = px.sunburst(df, path=['continent', 'country', 'city'], values='prizes')
The first column in path is the inner ring; each ring splits its parent slice.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict what the inner and outer rings show; reorder path for a target chart.

topics.title: Statistical tests with scipy.stats
topics.summary: Call scipy.stats test functions, read or unpack their statistic and p-value, and avoid NaN results from missing data.

knowledge_points.title: from scipy import stats; read .statistic and .pvalue
knowledge_points.worked_example:
from scipy import stats
result = stats.ttest_ind([8, 9, 7, 10, 9], [5, 6, 7, 5, 6])
print(round(result.statistic, 2), round(result.pvalue, 4))   # 4.43 0.0022
scipy is organised in subpackages; stats holds the tests.
knowledge_points.practice: Write the import and the test call; predict which attribute holds the p-value.

knowledge_points.title: The result unpacks like a tuple
knowledge_points.practice: Unpack test results into names; fix an unpacking in the wrong order.

knowledge_points.title: Correlation with a p-value: pearsonr
knowledge_points.worked_example:
r, p = stats.pearsonr([1, 2, 3, 4, 5], [2, 4, 5, 4, 5])
print(round(r, 2), round(p, 2))   # 0.77 0.12
A strong-looking r from 5 points can still be weak evidence.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the sign of r for described data; decide whether a given p-value is below 0.05.

knowledge_points.title: NaN in, NaN out
knowledge_points.worked_example:
import numpy as np
result = stats.ttest_ind([1, 2, np.nan], [3, 4, 5])
print(result.pvalue)   # nan
Drop missing values first (a mask or dropna), or pass nan_policy='omit'.
knowledge_points.practice: Fix a test that returns nan; write the mask that removes NaN before testing.

topics.title: Describing a distribution: centre, spread and shape
topics.summary: Compute standard deviation (and know NumPy's ddof=0 vs pandas' ddof=1), recognise skew from mean vs median and from a histogram, apply the 68-95-99.7 rule, and compute z-scores.

knowledge_points.title: Standard deviation, and ddof
knowledge_points.worked_example:
x = np.array([2, 4, 4, 4, 5, 5, 7, 9])
print(x.std())                    # 2.0
print(round(x.std(ddof=1), 2))    # 2.14
NumPy divides by n by default; statistics.stdev and pandas .std() divide by n - 1 (ddof=1).
knowledge_points.practice: Predict which call gives which value; fix a comparison of NumPy and pandas spreads that disagree.

knowledge_points.title: Shape: symmetric or skewed
knowledge_points.worked_example:
incomes: mean 58,000, median 41,000 -> long right tail (a few very high values)
heights: mean 170, median 170 -> roughly symmetric
A histogram shows the same thing: the tail stretches towards the side the mean is pulled to.
knowledge_points.practice: Classify histograms and mean/median pairs as symmetric, right- or left-skewed.

knowledge_points.title: The normal distribution and 68-95-99.7
knowledge_points.worked_example:
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
x = rng.normal(loc=100, scale=15, size=10_000)
print(round(((x > 85) & (x < 115)).mean(), 2))   # 0.68
About 68% of a normal distribution lies within 1 std of the mean, 95% within 2, 99.7% within 3.
knowledge_points.practice: Estimate the share of values in a range for a normal distribution with given mean and std.

knowledge_points.title: z-scores: how many stds from the mean
knowledge_points.practice: Compute z-scores by hand; write the mask that flags unusual values.

topics.title: Null hypothesis and p-values, by shuffling
topics.summary: State a null hypothesis for a difference between two groups, estimate a p-value by shuffling group labels, and interpret it correctly.

knowledge_points.title: The null hypothesis: 'no real difference'
knowledge_points.worked_example:
before = [12, 15, 11, 14, 13]   # % deaths per month
after = [8, 9, 11, 7, 10]
observed = statistics.mean(before) - statistics.mean(after)
print(observed)   # 4
Null hypothesis: the change made no difference, and 4 is just luck in which months landed where.
knowledge_points.practice: Write the null hypothesis for described studies; compute the observed difference.

knowledge_points.title: Shuffle the labels to see what luck alone does
knowledge_points.worked_example:
random.seed(1)
pooled = before + after
extreme = 0
for _ in range(10_000):
    random.shuffle(pooled)
    diff = statistics.mean(pooled[:5]) - statistics.mean(pooled[5:])
    if diff >= observed:
        extreme += 1
print(extreme / 10_000)   # 0.0093
knowledge_points.practice: Order the lines of a permutation test; predict how the p-value changes if the groups overlap more.

knowledge_points.title: Reading a p-value
knowledge_points.worked_example:
p = 0.0093: if there were no real difference, a gap this big would appear in under 1% of shuffles.
p < 0.05 -> reject the null hypothesis.
p is NOT the chance the null is true; p > 0.05 does NOT prove the groups are equal.
knowledge_points.practice: Pick the correct reading of given p-values; spot false statements about p-values.

topics.title: Comparing two groups with a t-test
topics.summary: Split a DataFrame into two groups, run a two-sample t-test, decide at the 0.05 level, and report the size of the difference alongside the p-value.

knowledge_points.title: Split the data into two groups
knowledge_points.worked_example:
df = pd.DataFrame({'washing': ['no'] * 5 + ['yes'] * 5,
                   'pct_deaths': [8, 9, 7, 10, 9, 5, 6, 7, 5, 6]})
before = df[df['washing'] == 'no']['pct_deaths']
after = df[df['washing'] == 'yes']['pct_deaths']
print(before.mean(), after.mean())   # 8.6 5.8
knowledge_points.practice: Write the masks that split a table into two groups; predict the group means.

knowledge_points.title: Run the t-test and decide
knowledge_points.worked_example:
t, p = stats.ttest_ind(before, after)
print(round(p, 4))   # 0.0022
print(p < 0.05)      # True: significant at the 0.05 level
The t-test does in one call what the shuffling simulation estimated.
knowledge_points.practice: Write the test and the decision line; predict the decision for given p-values and thresholds.

knowledge_points.title: Report the size of the effect too
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print(round(before.mean() - after.mean(), 1))   # 2.8 percentage points
With huge samples a tiny, unimportant difference can be 'significant'; always give the difference itself.
knowledge_points.practice: Choose the better report of a result; judge whether a significant result matters in practice.

knowledge_points.title: Unequal spreads: Welch's t-test
knowledge_points.worked_example:
t, p = stats.ttest_ind(before, after, equal_var=False)
The default assumes both groups have similar spread; equal_var=False drops that assumption.
knowledge_points.practice: Decide from two stds whether to pass equal_var=False; fill in the call.

topics.title: The scikit-learn pattern: create, fit, predict
topics.summary: Create a model, fit it on a 2D feature table and a target, predict new values, read learned attributes, and split data into training and test sets.

knowledge_points.title: Create, fit, predict
knowledge_points.worked_example:
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
X = pd.DataFrame({'hours': [1, 2, 3, 4]})
y = pd.Series([52, 54, 56, 58])
model = LinearRegression()
model.fit(X, y)
print(model.predict(pd.DataFrame({'hours': [5]})))   # [60.]
knowledge_points.practice: Order the create/fit/predict lines; predict the output for exactly linear data.

knowledge_points.title: X must be 2D: a table, not a single column
knowledge_points.worked_example:
model.fit([1, 2, 3, 4], y)
# ValueError: Expected 2D array, got 1D array instead: ...
Use df[['hours']] (double brackets) or [[1], [2], [3], [4]]; df['hours'] is 1D and fails too.
knowledge_points.practice: Fix fit and predict calls that pass 1D data; predict the shape of df[['a']] vs df['a'].

knowledge_points.title: Learned attributes end in _
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print(round(model.coef_[0], 2), round(model.intercept_, 2))   # 2.0 50.0
coef_ and intercept_ exist only after fit; on an unfitted model:
# AttributeError: 'LinearRegression' object has no attribute 'coef_'
knowledge_points.practice: Predict learned attributes for exactly linear data; fix code that reads coef_ before fit.

knowledge_points.title: Hold out test data with train_test_split
knowledge_points.worked_example:
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.25, random_state=0)
print(len(X_train), len(X_test))   # 3 1
The four results come back in this order; random_state makes the split repeatable.
knowledge_points.practice: Fix an unpacking in the wrong order; predict split sizes for given test_size values.

topics.title: Lines of best fit: slope, intercept and residuals
topics.summary: Predict with y = slope * x + intercept, compute residuals and the sum of squared residuals, compare candidate lines, and fit one with np.polyfit.

knowledge_points.title: A line predicts y from x
knowledge_points.worked_example:
x = np.array([1, 2, 3])
pred = 3 * x + 10
print(pred)   # [13 16 19]
slope 3: each extra unit of x adds 3 to y; intercept 10: the prediction at x = 0.
knowledge_points.practice: Compute predictions from a slope and intercept; read slope and intercept off a plotted line.

knowledge_points.title: Residuals: actual minus predicted
knowledge_points.worked_example:
y = np.array([14, 15, 20])
resid = y - pred
print(resid, (resid ** 2).sum())   # [ 1 -1  1] 3
Points above the line have positive residuals.
knowledge_points.practice: Compute residuals and their squared sum; mark points above or below a line on a scatter plot.

knowledge_points.title: Least squares: the smallest squared error wins
knowledge_points.worked_example:
resid2 = y - (3 * x + 11)
print(resid2, (resid2 ** 2).sum())   # [ 0 -2  0] 4
3x + 10 (total 3) fits better than 3x + 11 (total 4), even though 3x + 11 hits two points exactly.
knowledge_points.practice: Compare candidate lines by squared error; explain why residuals are squared before summing.

knowledge_points.title: Fit the best line with np.polyfit
knowledge_points.worked_example:
slope, intercept = np.polyfit(x, y, 1)
print(round(slope, 2), round(intercept, 2))   # 3.0 10.33
Degree 1 means a straight line; plot it over plt.scatter(x, y) to check the fit.
knowledge_points.practice: Write the polyfit call and unpack its result; predict a value from the fitted line.

topics.title: Fitting and judging a regression with scikit-learn
topics.summary: Fit a one-feature linear regression, state what the slope means in context, judge the fit with R-squared, and recognise unsafe extrapolation.

knowledge_points.title: Fit and state the slope in words
knowledge_points.worked_example:
X = pd.DataFrame({'budget': [10, 20, 30, 40]})   # $ millions
y = [25, 45, 70, 80]
model = LinearRegression().fit(X, y)
print(round(model.coef_[0], 2), round(model.intercept_, 2))   # 1.9 7.5
Each extra $1M of budget goes with about $1.9M more revenue.
knowledge_points.practice: Write the interpretation of a fitted slope with units; predict revenue for a given budget.

knowledge_points.title: R-squared with score
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print(round(model.score(X, y), 2))   # 0.98
R-squared is the share of the variation in y the line explains: 1 is a perfect fit, 0 no better than the mean.
knowledge_points.practice: Rank fits by R-squared; compute R-squared from given squared-error totals.

knowledge_points.title: Do not trust the line far outside the data
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print(model.predict(pd.DataFrame({'budget': [0]})))   # [7.5]
A film with no budget earning $7.5M is not a real prediction: the data started at $10M.
knowledge_points.practice: Decide which predictions are interpolation and which are risky extrapolation.

topics.title: Several features, log transforms and residual checks
topics.summary: Fit a regression on several features and read one coefficient per column, model a skewed target in log units and convert predictions back, and check residuals for patterns.

knowledge_points.title: One coefficient per feature
knowledge_points.worked_example:
X = pd.DataFrame({'rooms': [2, 3, 4, 3], 'dist': [1, 2, 1, 4]})
y = [18, 21, 28, 17]
model = LinearRegression().fit(X, y)
print(round(model.coef_[0], 2), round(model.coef_[1], 2))   # 5.0 -2.0
Coefficients follow the column order: +5 per room, -2 per km, holding the other fixed.
knowledge_points.practice: Pair coefficients with column names; interpret the sign of each.

knowledge_points.title: Skewed target: fit log(price), convert back with exp
knowledge_points.worked_example:
df['log_price'] = np.log(df['price'])
model.fit(X, df['log_price'])
log_pred = model.predict(new_house)
print(np.exp(log_pred))   # back in dollars
Forgetting np.exp reports a 'price' of about 12.
knowledge_points.practice: Fix code that reports log-scale predictions as prices; choose when a log transform helps.

knowledge_points.title: Residuals should look like random noise
knowledge_points.worked_example:
resid = y - model.predict(X)
plt.scatter(model.predict(X), resid)
Residuals centred on 0 with no pattern: the line fits. A curve or funnel shape means a missing feature or a transform is needed.
knowledge_points.practice: Classify residual plots as fine or problematic; compute residuals for small data.
